questions.prompt: What is the goal of finding 'good classes' of CQs in this lecture?
options: Restrict query structure to make combined evaluation tractable
Fix only the database while allowing arbitrary queries
Fix only the number of output tuples rather than the body structure
Only reorder atoms without changing the query's structural class
questions.explanation: Graph or hypergraph structure can make evaluation easier even when Q is part of the input. The goal is not to change semantics or merely rename variables.

questions.prompt: Bounded treewidth is a property of which object here?
options: A hypergraph measured only by its number of hyperedges, ignoring connections
The graph of the CQ
The number of tuples in the largest relation
The physical height of a B+ tree
questions.explanation: Treewidth measures the structure of the variable-interaction graph, not the height of an index tree. These uses of 'tree' describe different concepts.

questions.prompt: What does bounded hypertree width describe?
options: The largest tuple count of any relation
The number of head variables, ignoring the body
How close the CQ's hypergraph is to being acyclic
A fixed number of columns in every atom, ignoring shared variables
questions.explanation: Hypertree width measures hypergraph structure. It is neither a storage-size measure nor simply a restriction that all atoms have the same arity.

questions.prompt: What hypertree width is stated for acyclic CQs?
options: 0 for every query with at least one atom
The number of atoms, regardless of their connections
The number of variables in the largest atom in every case
questions.explanation: The lecture introduces acyclic CQs as having hypertree width 1. Data cardinality does not determine the structural width of a query.

questions.prompt: Why does PTIME evaluation for a fixed query not already meet lecture 25's goal?
options: The lecture seeks good guarantees for varying input queries with suitable structure
The fixed-query PTIME result is false for every CQ
PTIME means every query takes the same amount of time
Every query with more than two atoms is undecidable
questions.explanation: Data complexity fixes Q, whereas these good classes target combined complexity. This does not contradict the earlier fixed-query result.

questions.prompt: Which hyperedge corresponds to the atom R(x,y,z)?
options: Three separate edges {x,y},{y,z},{x,z} in place of a hyperedge
The set {x,y,z}
A node named R that contains no variables
The set of every value currently stored in database relation R
questions.explanation: The hypergraph retains the atom's whole variable set as one edge. A three-edge clique represents the primal graph and has a different edge structure.

questions.prompt: What does the running-intersection condition require in a join tree?
options: Every atom has the same number of variables
Every pair of atoms shares at least one variable
For each variable, all nodes containing it form a connected subtree
Every variable occurs in exactly one atom
questions.explanation: A variable may occur in many atoms, but the path between them must also consist of nodes containing that variable. Not every pair of atoms needs to overlap.

questions.prompt: Which join tree is valid for R(a,b),S(b,c),T(c,d)?
options: R—T—S
S—R—T
Every tree is valid
R—S—T
questions.explanation: R—S—T keeps the nodes containing b connected, and likewise for c. Placing T between R and S would break the connectedness of b.

questions.prompt: Is the hypergraph {a,b},{b,c},{c,a} acyclic?
options: No; every tree connecting the three edges violates running intersection for some variable
Yes, because it has only three edges
Yes, because each edge has exactly two variables
It cannot be assessed without a database
questions.explanation: Acyclicity is a property of query structure. This triangle creates a running-intersection conflict regardless of the current data.

questions.prompt: What can adding {a,b,c} to the triangle {a,b},{b,c},{c,a} do?
options: It must remain cyclic because adding a hyperedge can never help
Make the hypergraph acyclic by using the large edge as the join-tree center
Make it necessarily more cyclic because the number of hyperedges increases
Make it acyclic only if all three smaller edges are deleted first
questions.explanation: Hypergraph acyclicity differs from ordinary graph acyclicity: the large central edge contains every shared variable. Ordinary graph rules about adding edges do not transfer directly.

questions.prompt: Which GYO reduction rule is valid?
options: Delete any variable occurring in two edges
Delete all output variables first
Delete a variable occurring in at most one hyperedge
Delete the largest edge regardless of containment
questions.explanation: A variable occurring in only one edge cannot connect that edge cyclically to others. Arbitrarily deleting a degree-2 variable can give an incorrect conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which hyperedge may GYO delete?
options: Any edge with the largest number of variables
Any edge that is a leaf in an arbitrary tree
Any edge intersecting at least one other edge
An empty edge or an edge contained in another edge
questions.explanation: A contained edge adds no structural requirement that must be retained for this acyclicity test. Merely intersecting another edge is not sufficient for deletion.

questions.prompt: What does reducing H to the empty hypergraph with GYO establish?
options: H is acyclic
The query is semantically equivalent to the empty query
The database contains no tuples
The query must return YES on every database
questions.explanation: GYO tests structure; it does not rewrite an executable query by discarding all its atoms while preserving meaning. The empty hypergraph says nothing about the data.

questions.prompt: For H={a,b},{b,c},{c,d}, what remains after removing a and d?
options: The same three edges, unchanged
{b},{b,c},{c}, after which the contained edges can be removed
The triangle {a,b},{b,c},{c,a}
Only {a,d}
questions.explanation: a and d each occur in only one edge, so they may be removed. The remaining singleton edges are contained in {b,c}, allowing reduction to continue.

questions.prompt: GYO stops at a nonempty structure with no applicable rule. What follows?
options: Reordering database tuples will make it acyclic
It is acyclic because at least one variable was removed
The hypergraph is cyclic
Nothing can be concluded until the query runs on a database
questions.explanation: The theorem states that a hypergraph is acyclic exactly when it reduces to empty. The test does not depend on tuple order or evaluation on a particular database.

questions.prompt: What does the O(size(D)·size(Q)) guarantee apply to in this lecture's setting?
options: Printing an arbitrarily large output without accounting for output size
Every CQ, including cyclic ones
Every SQL query with arbitrary recursion
The decision or membership problem for acyclic CQs
questions.explanation: Enumerating the output may cost more than this bound because the output itself can be large. The stated context is decision evaluation, with acyclicity as an essential condition.

questions.prompt: For fixed acyclic Q, how does O(size(D)·size(Q)) grow with size(D)?
options: Linearly in size(D) within this bound
Quadratically, because size(Q) always equals size(D)
Exponentially in size(D)
Independently of the data
questions.explanation: Fixing Q makes size(Q) a constant. Query size must not be equated with database size.

questions.prompt: If both size(D) and size(Q) double, by what factor does the product in O(size(D)·size(Q)) change?
options: About 2, because each factor is individually linear
About 4 in the product expression
About 8
It stays unchanged
questions.explanation: (2size(D))(2size(Q))=4size(D)size(Q). Being linear in each argument separately does not mean being linear in their sum when both grow together.

questions.prompt: Why can evaluating an acyclic CQ be easier than evaluating a general CQ?
options: Acyclic CQs have no joins
Every relation contains only one tuple
The join tree allows local information to be combined with global guarantees
Acyclic CQs have no existential variables
questions.explanation: An acyclic CQ can still have many joins and existential variables. Its favorable dependency structure supports efficient dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: A CQ has a join tree, but its output is a large product of two independent relations. Can enumeration ignore the cost of writing the output?
options: Yes, because an acyclic CQ returns at most one tuple
Yes, because GYO has removed its edges
No, because acyclic evaluation is undecidable
No; enumeration must at least account for the number of results produced
questions.explanation: Decision and enumeration are different tasks. Acyclicity does not itself bound the cardinality of a non-Boolean result.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the Boolean algorithm presented?
options: Find a join tree for the query hypergraph
Materialize the entire join before finding a join tree
Perform semijoins in any atom order without using the structure
Choose a root and discard every relation in its branches
questions.explanation: The join tree determines how semijoin information is propagated. Discarding atoms arbitrarily changes the query.

questions.prompt: Which schema does the semijoin R ⋉ S return?
options: All columns of R and S, as in a full joined tuple
Only R's columns, retaining tuples that have a match in S
Only S's columns
One COUNT column for every tuple
questions.explanation: A semijoin filters left-hand tuples by whether they have a match. It does not construct the fully combined tuples of a join.

questions.prompt: Let R(B)={1,2}, S(B,C)={(1,k),(2,m)}, T(C)={k}, with join tree R—S—T rooted at R. What is the root after the bottom-up pass?
options: The empty set
questions.explanation: S⋉T retains (1,k), then R⋉S retains 1. Looking only at the original S would incorrectly retain 2 as well.

questions.prompt: After the bottom-up semijoin pass, the root is empty. What does the Boolean CQ return?
options: YES, because the original tables were nonempty
It is still unknown; the entire full join must be printed
YES, if the smallest relation was chosen as the root
NO
questions.explanation: An empty root means no remaining tuple can extend to a match across the whole tree. Nonempty input tables alone do not guarantee that their join has a match.

questions.prompt: Why is it safe to combine witnesses from different branches of a join tree?
options: Running intersection ensures that shared variables are connected through nodes that also contain them
Different branches can never share a variable
Semijoins generate every possible combination to check
The root always contains every query variable
questions.explanation: A variable shared by different branches must also occur in the intermediate nodes on their path. This ensures compatibility of the choices; the root need not contain every variable.
